title: Give Thanks
subtitle: When Gratitude Becomes Generosity
tagline: Gratitude recognizes what was given. Generosity helps it reach someone else.
headline: When Gratitude Becomes Generosity
headline_sub: What We Receive Was Never Meant to End With Us
seo_title: Gratitude and Generosity: When What You Receive Keeps Moving
seo_description: God provides, we give, and thanksgiving rises to God. A Thanksgiving devotional for men on letting what you’ve received keep moving, starting at your own table.
og_image_alt: When Gratitude Becomes Generosity: Gratitude recognizes what was given. Generosity helps it reach someone else. TheWrkShop.

scriptures.text: And God is able to bless you abundantly, so that in all things at all times, having all that you need, you will abound in every good work.
You will be enriched in every way so that you can be generous on every occasion, and through us your generosity will result in thanksgiving to God.

blocks.text: Paul describes an extraordinary movement.
Notice the direction.
The gift does not stop with the person who receives it.
It moves outward.
GRATITUDE RECOGNIZES THE GIFT. GENEROSITY KEEPS IT MOVING.
Paul was writing about money for believers in need. The same pattern holds for everything God puts in our hands.
What happens when those gifts are used to serve others?
“WHAT I’VE RECEIVED IS MAINLY FOR ME.”
Imagine a man whose career took off because a mentor invested in him.
Years later, he is influential himself.
He could mentor someone else.
But instead, he protects every advantage.
The gift stops moving.
Or imagine a man who received extraordinary compassion during a hard season.
Later he meets someone else who is struggling.
He remembers what helped him.
But he chooses not to get involved.
GRATITUDE STAYED A FEELING. IT NEVER BECAME GENEROSITY.
Why do we hold so tightly to what we’ve received?
One question gets underneath it:
What am I afraid will run out if I give it away?
Time? Money? Advantage? Credit? Importance?
Sometimes the honest answer is real limits. Generosity still requires wisdom and boundaries.
But sometimes we hold tightly because we’ve forgotten that what we have was entrusted to us.
WHEN A GIFT BECOMES PART OF OUR IDENTITY, SHARING IT CAN FEEL LIKE LOSING OURSELVES.
That deserves examination.
GOD’S PROVISION MAKES US PARTICIPANTS IN HIS CARE FOR OTHERS.
Gratitude and generosity belong together: one receives the gift, the other passes it on.
Paul’s emphasis is willing generosity rooted in God’s grace.
The goal is not personal recognition.
It is provision that serves people and results in thanksgiving to God.
That changes the question.
Instead of asking only, “What have I received?”
We start asking, “What am I now able to give?”

items: What have I received that someone else now needs?
Who invested in me without expecting anything back?
What knowledge am I holding onto?
Where has fear made me unnecessarily protective?
Has my gratitude changed how I treat people?

blocks.text: Thanksgiving is two days away.
Is there someone who will be alone on Thursday? A neighbor, a coworker, a man from your group, a widow from church?
Invite them to your table.
That’s gratitude becoming generosity this week.
Then choose one more gift you’ve received, and one person who could benefit from it.
And let the thanks go back to God.
Gratitude recognizes what was given. Generosity helps it reach someone else.

Father, thank You for every gift You have entrusted to me. Keep me from treating blessings as possessions to protect rather than opportunities to serve. Give me wisdom, generosity, and joy in helping others. May what I receive become a blessing beyond me. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
Gratitude recognizes the gift; generosity keeps it moving.
A blessing can become an opportunity to bless someone else.
What you received may be exactly what another person now needs.
Who will be alone on Thursday?
—TheWrkShop
